title: Generative AI for Video and Audio
description: The newest and least predictable kinds of generation, and how to work with them anyway.

lessons.title: Text-to-video
lessons.description: The least reliable of the five kinds, and how to prompt around its limits.
lessons.content:
> Video and audio generation is the fastest-moving area in this course. Specific tools, quality levels and limits change within months. This lesson covers what the technique is **for** and where it breaks, which is stable. Check what any tool currently does before you rely on it.

## Learn

Text-to-video generates a short clip from a description. It is the newest of the five kinds from module 1 and by some distance the least reliable.

### How it differs from images

An image needs to look right once. A video needs to look right in every frame **and** be consistent between them.

That second requirement is the whole difficulty. A face that shifts slightly between frames, a hand that gains a finger, a background object that moves when nothing touched it -- all read as obviously wrong to a human eye, even when each individual frame would pass as a still.

So video generation is not image generation repeated. It is a harder problem, and it shows.

### What the tools actually produce

Broadly: **short clips**. A few seconds, sometimes longer. Not scenes, not sequences, not films.

Quality varies enormously by subject. Some things work well:

- Slow camera moves over landscapes or objects
- Abstract and atmospheric material
- Simple single-subject motion
- Anything where small inconsistencies are not noticeable

Some things do not:

- People doing anything specific with their hands
- Several people interacting
- Anything needing exact continuity between shots
- Text that must stay readable
- Precise physical cause and effect

### Prompting for video

Everything from module 7 applies, plus **motion**.

The additional ingredients:

**Camera movement.** Slow pan left, dolly in, static shot, aerial drone shot, handheld. Camera motion is one of the more reliable things you can control.

**Subject movement.** What moves and how. "Leaves drifting slowly", "steam rising".

**Pace.** Slow, gradual, gentle. Fast and complex motion degrades quality noticeably, so where you have a choice, choose slow.

> Static shot, a ceramic cup of coffee on a wooden table by a rain-streaked window, steam rising slowly, grey afternoon light, shallow depth of field

Note what is not being asked for: nobody is moving, nothing complicated is happening, and the camera is still. That is a prompt designed around the limits.

### The realistic workflow

**Generate several. Expect most to fail.** A hit rate of one in four or five good clips is normal. This is not you doing it wrong.

**Keep clips short.** Quality degrades over length.

**Plan for cutting.** Several short generated clips edited together works far better than trying to generate one longer piece.

**Use it where it suits.** Backgrounds, atmosphere, transitions, B-roll. Not the shot that has to carry the meaning.

### Where this genuinely helps today

**Background and atmosphere** behind titles or narration.

**Establishing shots** where nothing specific has to happen.

**Concept and mood pieces** where the point is the feel.

**Placeholder material** while you arrange the real thing.

What it does not yet replace is footage where something specific must happen, correctly, with real people.

## Demonstrate

Calibrate your expectations properly. Take any video tool and generate two prompts, four clips each.

**Prompt one, designed for the limits.**

> Static shot, morning mist drifting slowly across a still lake, distant trees, soft grey light

**Prompt two, designed against them.**

> A woman sitting at a desk writes a note on paper, folds it, and hands it to a man standing beside her

Watch all eight. Prompt one will probably give you two or three usable clips. Prompt two will probably give you none, and the failures will be instructive: hands, the paper, the handover, the continuity.

That contrast is the current state of the technology, and seeing it directly is worth more than any description.

## Practice

Pick something you might actually want a short clip for -- a background for a title, an atmosphere shot, a social post.

Write a prompt deliberately designed around the limits: slow motion, simple subject, controlled camera, nothing requiring hands or continuity.

Generate six. Count how many are usable.

Then write one sentence on what you would have to do differently if you needed the difficult version -- and the honest answer is usually to film it.

## What to remember

- Video must be consistent between frames, not just right once; that is the whole difficulty
- Expect a hit rate around one in four or five, and generate accordingly
- Slow motion, simple subjects and controlled camera moves work best
- People doing specific things with their hands remains unreliable
- Use it for atmosphere and background, not for the shot that carries the meaning

lessons.title: Image-to-video
lessons.description: Control the first frame and only the motion is uncertain.
lessons.content:
> This area moves fast: check what any tool currently does before relying on it.

## Learn

Image-to-video animates a still you supply. You give a picture and a description of the motion, and get a short clip that starts from it.

### Why it is usually better than text-to-video

**You control the first frame completely.**

With text-to-video you are gambling on composition, subject, style and motion all at once. With image-to-video you have already settled everything except the motion -- often using an image you generated carefully in module 7, or a real photograph.

That is one variable instead of five, and the results are correspondingly more usable.

### The practical workflow

1. **Generate or choose a still** you are happy with. Take the time here; everything depends on it.
2. **Describe only the motion.** Not the scene -- that already exists.
3. **Ask for little.** The less that moves, the better it holds together.
4. **Generate several.** Same as everywhere.

The motion prompt is short:

> Slow push in. Steam rises gently from the cup. Rain continues on the window. Nothing else moves.

That last sentence is worth adding routinely. Explicitly pinning everything else down reduces the stray motion that makes clips look wrong.

### What animates well

**Natural continuous motion.** Water, smoke, steam, cloud, fire, leaves, fabric in wind, rain.

**Slow camera moves** on a static scene. Push in, pull out, gentle pan, slight parallax.

**Subtle life** in an otherwise still scene. Small movements that make a photograph feel alive.

### What does not

**People doing things.** Same as text-to-video.

**Anything where an object must maintain its shape** through significant movement.

**Motion you describe precisely.** "He turns his head to the left and smiles" is a specification, and specifications are not what these tools respond to.

**Long clips.** Quality falls away.

### Where this fits

Image-to-video is currently the most practically useful video technique for most people, precisely because it is the most controlled.

A generated image from module 7, animated gently, makes a better social post, title background or slide element than either a still or a text-to-video clip -- and it takes minutes.

## Demonstrate

Take one image you generated in module 7. Animate it four ways:

1. *"Slow push in. Nothing in the scene moves."*
2. *"Gentle pan to the right. Nothing in the scene moves."*
3. Motion appropriate to the image -- steam, water, cloud, fabric, whatever is actually there -- plus *"Nothing else moves."*
4. Something ambitious: a person moving, an object changing, several things at once.

Watch all four. One, two and three will likely be usable. Four probably will not.

The lesson is the same as the last one, in a more controlled form: **the less you ask for, the more you get**.

## Practice

Build one finished five-second clip you would actually use.

Generate a still deliberately, using module 7's vocabulary. Then animate it, generating at least four attempts and picking the best.

Then do the honest test: watch it three times in a row, looking specifically for the frame where something goes wrong. There usually is one, and you want to know whether it is noticeable enough to matter.

## What to remember

- You control the first frame completely, which removes most of the gamble
- Describe only the motion, and add "nothing else moves"
- Water, smoke, steam, cloud, fabric and slow camera moves animate well
- Precise specified actions do not; these are not instructions
- Currently the most practically useful video technique for most people

lessons.title: AI avatars
lessons.description: Where a synthetic presenter works, where it backfires, and the consent rule.
lessons.content:
> This area moves fast: check what any tool currently does before relying on it.

## Learn

An AI avatar is a generated person who appears to speak. You supply a script; the output is video of a presenter delivering it.

### The two kinds

**Stock avatars.** A library of generated or licensed presenters. Pick one, type a script, get a video. No filming.

**Cloned avatars.** Built from footage of a real person, usually you, so the video looks like you presenting something you never filmed.

### Where it genuinely works

**Internal training and explanatory material.** Content that needs to exist, needs to be updated often, and does not need to be compelling. Regenerating a video because a policy changed is much cheaper than refilming.

**Multilingual versions.** The same content delivered in several languages, which would otherwise mean several presenters.

**Scale.** Personalised or numerous videos where filming each is impossible.

**Consistency.** Every video looks the same, which for a series of short internal explainers is a feature.

### Where it does not

**Anything requiring a genuine human connection.** Welcome messages, condolences, apologies, leadership communications in a difficult moment. An avatar delivering these reads as insincere, and often does more damage than sending text.

**Anything where being you is the point.**

**Content that has to hold attention.** Avatars are still slightly wrong in ways viewers notice without identifying -- timing, micro-expression, gesture. It is tiring to watch for long.

### The honesty rule

**Tell people.**

If a viewer would assume they are watching a real person and they are not, say so. A short line on screen or in the description is enough.

This is not a legal opinion; the rules vary by place and are changing. It is a practical position: being discovered to have used a synthetic presenter without saying so damages trust far more than saying so would have cost.

And with cloned avatars, one rule has no exceptions: **never make an avatar of someone without their explicit, informed consent.** Not a colleague, not a public figure, not for a joke. Lesson 6 of module 10 covers why in more detail, but the short version is that this is the technique behind the most harmful uses of generative AI.

### Practical quality notes

- **Write for speech.** Short sentences. Read your script aloud first.
- **Add pauses.** Most tools honour punctuation and explicit breaks. Unbroken delivery is the main giveaway.
- **Keep it short.** Under two minutes. The uncanny quality accumulates.
- **Check pronunciation** of names, acronyms and technical terms. Most tools let you correct these.

## Demonstrate

Generate two versions of the same sixty-second script, if you have access to a tool with a free tier.

**Version one:** the script as you would write it for reading -- longer sentences, written register.

**Version two:** the same content rewritten for speech. Short sentences. Deliberate pauses. Contractions. One idea per sentence.

Watch both. Version two will be noticeably better, and the difference is entirely in the writing rather than the tool.

Then show version two to someone without explaining what it is, and ask what they thought of the presenter. Record what they say. This tells you more about whether it is fit for your purpose than your own judgement will.

## Practice

Write a sixty-second script for something real -- an explanation, an announcement, a how-to.

Rewrite it for speech and read it aloud, timing yourself.

Then answer honestly, in writing: is an avatar the right format for this, or would text or a real recording serve better? For most personal or persuasive content the answer is no, and recognising that is the useful outcome of this lesson.

## What to remember

- Good for internal, updatable, multilingual and high-volume material
- Bad for anything needing genuine human connection or sustained attention
- Write for speech and add pauses; the writing matters more than the tool
- Disclose when a presenter is synthetic
- Never clone a person without their explicit, informed consent

lessons.title: AI voice generation
lessons.description: Narration, accessibility and drafts -- plus the code word conversation worth having.
lessons.content:
> This area moves fast: check what any tool currently does before relying on it.

## Learn

AI voice generation turns text into speech, and it has become good enough that most listeners cannot reliably tell.

### The two things it does

**Text to speech.** Choose a voice from a library and generate narration. No recording.

**Voice cloning.** Build a voice from a sample of someone speaking, then generate new speech in it.

The first is a normal production tool. The second carries real risk and is covered below.

### Where it genuinely helps

**Narration for video.** Much faster than recording, and trivially editable -- change a word without re-recording.

**Accessibility.** Audio versions of written material, which genuinely widens who can use it.

**Drafts.** Hearing a script read aloud reveals problems that reading silently hides. Even if a human records the final version, a generated draft is useful.

**Languages you do not speak.** With the same caution as any translation: have a speaker check it.

**Learning material** that people consume while doing something else.

### Getting good results

**Write for the ear.** Short sentences, one idea each, contractions. Text written for reading sounds wrong spoken.

**Punctuate for breath.** Commas and full stops become pauses. Most tools support explicit breaks. Unbroken delivery is the main giveaway of synthetic speech.

**Fix pronunciation.** Names, places, acronyms and technical terms need checking. Most tools allow corrections.

**Match voice to content.** Tools offer many voices; they are not interchangeable. Listen to several with your actual script.

**Listen to the whole thing.** Errors cluster in unusual words and numbers, and you will not catch them by skimming.

### Voice cloning: the rule

**Never clone a voice without the person's explicit, informed consent.**

Not a colleague's, not a family member's, not a public figure's, not as a joke.

Voice cloning needs very little source audio -- a short clip is often enough, and there is plenty of that for most people who have ever been recorded. It is the basis of a common and effective fraud: a familiar voice, urgently asking for money or credentials.

Two practical consequences:

**Do not do it.** Cloning your own voice for your own material is fine. Everything else needs consent, and in many places is unlawful without it.

**Tell the people close to you it exists.** A family code word for unexpected urgent requests is a simple and effective defence, and most people have never thought of it. This is genuinely worth doing after this lesson.

### Disclosure

The same position as avatars: if a listener would assume a human recorded it, say otherwise. A line in the description is enough.

## Demonstrate

Three exercises, twenty minutes.

**One: the writing difference.** Take a paragraph written for reading. Generate it as speech. Then rewrite it for the ear -- short sentences, contractions, deliberate pauses -- and generate again. The second will be substantially better and the tool did not change.

**Two: voice choice.** Take the same rewritten script and generate it in four different voices. Note how much the perceived meaning changes with delivery. Voice choice is a content decision, not a cosmetic one.

**Three: the failure hunt.** Write a short script containing a place name, an acronym, a date, a decimal and an unusual surname. Generate it and listen carefully.

Most people find at least one error, and they are always in exactly those categories. That is what to check every time.

## Practice

Produce one finished ninety-second narration for something real.

Write for the ear, punctuate for breath, choose a voice deliberately, fix pronunciations, and listen to the whole thing at least twice.

Then do the important non-technical part: **tell one person close to you that voice cloning exists and needs almost no source audio**, and agree a code word for unexpected urgent requests.

That two-minute conversation is the most practically protective thing in this entire course.

## What to remember

- Excellent for narration, accessibility, drafts and material in other languages
- Write for the ear and punctuate for breath; that matters more than the tool
- Errors cluster in names, acronyms, numbers and dates -- check those specifically
- Never clone a voice without explicit, informed consent
- Agree a code word with people close to you; cloning needs very little audio

lessons.title: AI music
lessons.description: Background that supports rather than competes, and an unsettled rights position.
lessons.content:
> This area moves fast: check what any tool currently does before relying on it.

## Learn

AI music tools generate audio from a description. Some produce instrumental pieces, some full tracks with vocals.

### What it is for

**Background music for video.** The main practical use. Music that supports something else without demanding attention.

**Placeholder tracks** while editing, before licensing the real thing.

**Filling a specific brief cheaply.** "Forty-five seconds, gentle, builds slightly, no vocals, ends cleanly" is a request that used to mean searching a library or paying someone.

**Experimentation** for people who make music, as a starting point rather than an output.

### Prompting for music

Similar to images: the vocabulary matters more than the technique.

**Genre and instrumentation.** Acoustic guitar, solo piano, lo-fi hip hop, orchestral strings, ambient synth.

**Tempo and energy.** Slow, mid-tempo, driving, gentle, sparse.

**Mood.** Warm, melancholy, hopeful, tense, neutral.

**Function.** "Background for a corporate explainer", "opening titles", "under narration". Stating the job helps more than people expect.

**Structure.** "Builds gradually", "consistent throughout, no big changes", "ends cleanly rather than fading".

> Gentle solo piano with light strings, slow tempo, warm and hopeful, suitable as background under narration, consistent energy with no dramatic changes, clean ending at 45 seconds

Note "under narration" and "no dramatic changes". Music that is interesting in its own right is bad background music, exactly as with poster backgrounds in module 7.

### The limitations

**Structure is weak.** Generated music often meanders. It rarely has the shape of a piece that goes somewhere and arrives.

**Length control is loose.** Asking for exactly forty-five seconds usually gets you approximately that. Plan to trim.

**Lyrics are generic** when tools generate them. Supply your own if they matter.

**It is derivative by construction.** Trained on existing music, it produces variations on what exists. This is fine for background and a poor route to anything original.

### The rights question

Genuinely unsettled, and worth being careful about.

**Check the tool's terms** for whether you may use output commercially. They differ substantially, and some restrict it on free tiers.

**Understand the training question is contested.** There is ongoing litigation and legislation about music models trained on copyrighted recordings. The legal position is not settled and may change.

**Platform rules differ from the tool's rules.** Some platforms have their own policies on AI-generated audio and their own detection. The tool saying you may use it does not mean a platform will accept it.

**For anything commercially significant**, licensed production music from an established library remains the lower-risk choice. The cost is small and the position is clear.

### The professional courtesy

If you are making something where a musician would normally be paid, and you use generated music instead, that is a decision with a consequence for someone. It may still be the right decision for your budget. It is worth making it knowingly rather than by default.

## Demonstrate

Generate background music for something real -- a video you have, a presentation, a podcast intro.

Write a prompt including all five ingredients: genre and instrumentation, tempo, mood, function, structure.

Generate at least four. Then do the actual test: **play each one under your content**, not on its own.

Music that sounded good alone is frequently wrong underneath, usually because it is too interesting. This test changes most people's choice.

## Practice

Produce one finished piece of background music for a real project.

Then answer three questions in writing:

1. What do this tool's terms say about commercial use?
2. What does the platform you will publish on say about AI-generated audio?
3. Would a licensed library track have been a better choice here, and why?

Question three deserves an honest answer. Sometimes it is yes.

## What to remember

- Best for background music that supports something else
- Name genre, instrumentation, tempo, mood, function and structure
- Test it under your content, not on its own
- Structure is weak and length control is loose; plan to trim
- The rights position is unsettled; check tool terms and platform rules separately

lessons.title: Writing a video script
lessons.description: Writing for the ear against a clock, where AI is unambiguously good.
lessons.content:
## Learn

This is the lesson in the module where AI is unambiguously good, because writing a script is a text task and text is what these models do best.

### Why scripts are different from other writing

**They are written to be heard, not read.** Different sentence length, different rhythm, different tolerance for complexity. A listener cannot go back a line.

**They have a clock.** Roughly 130 to 150 words a minute for clear narration. A two-minute video is about 280 words. This constraint is absolute and most first drafts ignore it.

**They compete with pictures.** If the visual shows it, the narration should not also say it.

### The structure that works for short video

**Hook, 5 seconds.** Why should anyone keep watching? A question, a surprising claim, a problem they recognise.

**Context, 15 seconds.** What is this about and why does it matter to them?

**Body, most of the time.** The actual content, in two or three points. Not five.

**Payoff, 10 seconds.** What they now know, or what to do next.

Most bad short videos fail at the hook and the count of points.

### Prompting for a script

Include the clock, the audience, the format and the structure:

> Write a script for a 90-second explainer video.
>
> Audience: first-year undergraduates who have never used a reference manager.
> Goal: they understand why one is worth setting up and install it today.
>
> Structure: 5-second hook, 15 seconds of context, three points, 10-second close with a specific action.
>
> Write for the ear: short sentences, one idea each, contractions. About 220 words total.
>
> Format: two columns, narration on the left and a note on what is on screen on the right.
>
> Do not narrate what the screen already shows.

The word count, the two-column format and the last line are what turn a generic output into a usable one.

### The iteration that matters

**Read it aloud and time it.** Always. Scripts that look fine are routinely thirty per cent too long, and that is the single most common problem.

Then:

> This is 40 seconds too long. Cut it to 220 words. Tell me what you removed, so I can overrule you.

The last clause is the useful one -- you get to keep something the model would have cut.

### Where AI helps beyond the first draft

**Tightening to a clock.** Mechanical and tedious; ideal.

**Rewriting for the ear.** Paste written prose and ask for the spoken version.

**Alternative hooks.** *"Give me eight different openings for this."* Hooks are the hardest part and volume genuinely helps.

**Shot notes.** From a finished script, suggesting what could be on screen.

**Checking against the visual.** *"Which lines say what the screen already shows?"*

### Where it does not

**It does not know your subject or your audience.** Generic scripts come from generic briefs.

**It does not have taste.** Hooks in particular need your judgement; generated ones tend toward the clichéd.

**It cannot tell you what will actually hold attention.** That is an empirical question about your audience.

## Demonstrate

Write a real 90-second script, in four steps.

1. Brief it properly, with audience, goal, structure, word count and the two-column format
2. **Read the result aloud and time it.** Note the actual duration
3. Ask for the cut to the right length, with the removals listed
4. Ask for eight alternative hooks and choose one yourself

Step 2 is the one to take seriously. The gap between the intended and actual duration is usually large, and discovering it now rather than in the edit saves real time.

## Practice

Take something you could genuinely explain in 90 seconds.

Run the four steps. Then read the final script aloud to another person and watch their face at the hook.

Record where their attention went. A hook that does not land is worth knowing about before you record anything.

## What to remember

- Around 130 to 150 words a minute; a two-minute video is about 280 words
- Hook, context, two or three points, payoff -- most failures are the hook or too many points
- Ask for narration and on-screen notes in two columns
- Always read aloud and time it; first drafts are routinely much too long
- Ask for eight hooks and choose yourself; the model has no taste

lessons.title: AI-assisted video editing
lessons.description: The quiet revolution: edit the transcript and the video follows.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Editing is where AI has quietly changed video production more than generation has, and it gets far less attention.

### What the tools actually do now

**Transcription and text-based editing.** The transcript is the timeline. Delete a sentence in the text and the video cuts. For anyone who edits talking-head content, this is the single largest change in years.

**Removing filler.** Ums, ahs, false starts, long pauses, in one pass.

**Automatic captions.** Fast, mostly accurate, and genuinely important for accessibility since a large share of viewers watch without sound.

**Reframing.** Converting a landscape recording to vertical, tracking the subject automatically.

**Silence removal.** Tightening pacing automatically.

**Audio cleanup.** Background noise removal, levelling, and making a poor recording noticeably better.

**Rough cuts from long footage.** Finding the usable takes in an hour of recording.

**Clip suggestion.** Identifying moments from a long video that might work as short clips.

### Why this matters more than generation

Generation produces material that mostly does not work. Editing tools do a job that was genuinely tedious, reliably, on your real footage.

For most people who make video, the practical value is overwhelmingly in this lesson rather than in the earlier ones. A two-hour edit becoming twenty minutes is a larger change than being able to generate a three-second clip of mist.

### The workflow that works now

1. **Record** normally, and do not worry much about small mistakes
2. **Transcribe** automatically
3. **Edit the transcript**, cutting whole sentences
4. **Remove filler and silence** automatically
5. **Clean the audio**
6. **Generate captions** and correct names and terms
7. **Reframe** for other formats if needed
8. **Add music**, generated or licensed
9. **Watch it properly**, start to finish, before publishing

Steps 2 to 7 used to be most of the work.

### What still needs you

**Judgement about what to keep.** The tools cut filler; they do not know which of your three explanations is the good one.

**Pacing and rhythm.** Automatic silence removal often produces something relentless. Some pauses are doing work.

**Correcting captions.** Names, technical terms and numbers are where transcription fails, exactly as with voice generation.

**Checking the reframe.** Automatic tracking sometimes crops out the thing that mattered.

**Watching the whole thing.** The most common cause of a bad published video is nobody watching it end to end.

### The caution

**Text-based editing makes it trivially easy to change meaning.** Removing "not" from a sentence is one keystroke and leaves no visible seam.

For your own material that is ordinary editing. For an interview or anything presented as a record, cutting so that someone appears to have said something they did not is a serious matter, and the ease of doing it accidentally is the point worth noting. Check the edited version of anything where someone else is speaking.

## Demonstrate

Take any video with speech -- record two minutes on your phone if you have nothing.

Run it through a transcript-based editor and do all of this:

1. Cut three sentences by deleting them from the transcript
2. Remove filler words automatically
3. Generate captions, then **read them carefully** and correct every name, term and number
4. Remove silences, then watch it back and ask whether the pacing now feels rushed
5. Reframe it vertically and check nothing important was cropped

Time the whole thing. Most people are surprised how fast it is, and equally surprised by how much correcting the captions still needed.

## Practice

Produce one finished, captioned, two-minute video of something real.

Then do the honest final step: watch it end to end, at normal speed, without touching anything. Note every problem you find.

Most people find at least two things they had not noticed while editing. Watching the whole thing is the step that most often gets skipped and most often matters.

## What to remember

- Transcript-based editing is the biggest practical change; edit the text, the video follows
- Automatic captions, filler removal, audio cleanup and reframing all work well
- Judgement about what to keep and how it should feel remains yours
- Always correct names, terms and numbers in captions
- Text-based editing makes changing someone's meaning trivially easy; check it
- Watch the whole thing before publishing

lessons.title: Practice questions and answer key
lessons.description: Ten questions covering the whole module, with a full explanation for each.
lessons.content:
Ten questions on the whole of module 8.

:::quiz
Q. Why is video generation harder than image generation?
- Video files are larger
+ Every frame must look right and be consistent with the frames around it
- Video models have fewer parameters
- Video prompts must be longer
= An image needs to be right once. A video needs consistency between frames, and small inconsistencies that would pass in a still read as obviously wrong in motion. It is a harder problem, not image generation repeated.

Q. Which prompt is designed around the current limits of text-to-video?
- Two people shaking hands and exchanging a document
+ Static shot, mist drifting slowly across a lake, soft grey light
- A chef chopping vegetables quickly
- A car driving past a shop with a readable sign
= Slow natural motion, a simple subject and a controlled camera work. Hands, interactions between people, fast complex motion and readable text do not.

Q. Why is image-to-video usually more reliable than text-to-video?
- It uses a more capable model
+ You control the first frame completely, so only the motion is uncertain
- It generates longer clips
- It requires less compute
= With text-to-video you gamble on composition, subject, style and motion at once. Starting from a still you already like leaves one variable instead of five.

Q. What is a useful line to add to almost any image-to-video motion prompt?
- "High quality, cinematic"
+ "Nothing else moves"
- "Make it look realistic"
- "Use smooth camera motion"
= Explicitly pinning everything else down reduces the stray motion that makes clips read as wrong. The less that moves, the better the clip holds together.

Q. When is an AI avatar the wrong choice?
- Internal training material that changes often
- The same explainer in five languages
+ A message that depends on genuine human connection, such as an apology
- A short how-to that will be updated quarterly
= An avatar delivering an apology or a condolence reads as insincere and usually does more damage than sending text would. Avatars suit content that needs to exist and be updated, not content that needs to land emotionally.

Q. What is the rule on voice cloning?
- It is fine for public figures since their voice is already public
+ Never clone a voice without the person's explicit, informed consent
- It is fine if you disclose it afterwards
- It is fine for short clips under thirty seconds
= Cloning needs very little source audio and is the basis of a common fraud. Your own voice for your own material is fine; everything else needs consent, and in many places is unlawful without it.

Q. What is the most practically protective thing to do after the voice lesson?
- Stop using voice generation tools
+ Tell people close to you that cloning exists, and agree a code word for unexpected urgent requests
- Register your voice with a detection service
- Only use voices from a stock library
= A familiar voice urgently asking for money or credentials is an effective and common scam. A family code word is simple, free, and most people have never thought of it.

Q. What makes generated music suitable as background?
- Being as interesting and memorable as possible
+ Consistent energy, no dramatic changes, and a stated function such as "under narration"
- The longest available duration
- Including vocals for engagement
= Music that is interesting in its own right is bad background music, exactly as a busy image makes a bad poster background. Always test it under your content rather than on its own.

Q. Roughly how many words is a two-minute video script?
- About 150
+ About 280
- About 450
- About 600
= Clear narration runs around 130 to 150 words a minute. First drafts are routinely thirty per cent too long, which is why reading aloud and timing it is not optional.

Q. Which AI capability has changed video production most in practice?
- Text-to-video generation
- AI avatars
+ Transcript-based editing, captions and audio cleanup
- AI music generation
= Generation produces material that mostly does not work yet. Editing tools do genuinely tedious jobs reliably on your real footage. A two-hour edit becoming twenty minutes is a larger change than generating three seconds of mist.
:::

## How to read your score

Seven or more and you are ready for module 9. If you missed questions here, the most useful thing is to actually run the calibration exercise in lesson 1 -- the state of video generation is something you need to have seen rather than read about.

lessons.title: Hands-on lab: a sixty-second explainer
lessons.description: Script, narration, visuals, captions and three tests.
lessons.content:
Fifty minutes. You will produce one finished, captioned sixty-second explainer video, combining everything in this module.

## Before you start

Pick something you can genuinely explain in sixty seconds. A concept from your field, how to do something, why something matters.

You need: a script, narration, some visuals, and an editor. Everything here can be done with free tiers.

## Step 1: The script

Brief it properly, using lesson 6:

- Audience, named specifically
- Goal: what they know or do afterwards
- Structure: 5-second hook, 15 seconds context, two points, 10-second close
- **About 145 words**
- Two columns: narration and on-screen notes
- "Do not narrate what the screen already shows"

Generate it, then **read it aloud and time it**. Record the actual duration.

Cut to length, asking for the removals to be listed so you can overrule.

## Step 2: Eight hooks

Ask for eight alternative openings. Choose one yourself.

Write down why you chose it. Generated hooks tend toward the clichéd, so this is a judgement call the tool cannot make.

## Step 3: The narration

Generate the voiceover, or record it yourself.

If generating: write for the ear, punctuate for breath, choose the voice deliberately, and check every name, acronym, number and date.

Listen to the whole thing at least twice.

## Step 4: The visuals

Produce visuals for each section. Any mix of:

- Stills generated using module 7's vocabulary
- Those stills animated gently with image-to-video
- Short text-to-video clips, if the subject suits the limits
- Screen recordings or real footage
- Plain text slides, which are often the right answer

:::hint My generated clips all look wrong
Expected -- a hit rate of one in four or five is normal. Two fixes. First, use image-to-video from a still you like rather than text-to-video, which removes most of the gamble. Second, reconsider whether you need moving pictures at all: a well-designed still held for four seconds under good narration is frequently better than a mediocre clip, and it is what a lot of professional explainer video actually does.
:::

## Step 5: Assemble

Edit it together. Narration first, visuals to fit.

Add background music, generated or licensed. Test it **under** the narration and set it low enough that every word is clear.

## Step 6: Captions

Generate them. Then read every caption and correct names, technical terms and numbers.

Do not skip this. A large share of viewers watch without sound, and the errors are always in exactly those categories.

## Step 7: Test it

1. **Watch it end to end** at normal speed without touching anything
2. **Watch it on a phone with the sound off**, reading only the captions. Does it still work?
3. **Show it to one person** and afterwards ask what the main point was. Do not tell them first.

Record what each test revealed.

## Step 8: Write it up

1. Your brief and final script, with the word count and timed duration
2. The eight hooks and why you chose yours
3. How the narration was produced and what you had to correct
4. Your visual approach, including how many clips you generated and how many you used
5. What each of the three tests revealed
6. What took longest, and what you would do differently

## What good looks like

A strong submission reports the **hit rate honestly**: how many clips were generated, how many were usable. "I generated 12 clips and used 3" is a real finding and the expected one.

It also takes the third test seriously. If your viewer could not say what the main point was, that is the most valuable thing you learned, and it is a script problem rather than a production one.

lessons.title: Assignment: a short video with a disclosure statement
lessons.description: A published video plus the disclosure reasoning, marked against a rubric.
lessons.content:
## The task

Produce a short video using generative tools, **published with a disclosure statement**, plus a written account of every AI-assisted decision.

The disclosure is not an afterthought here. It is half of what is being assessed, because deciding what to tell your audience is the skill this module most needs to teach.

## What to submit

A video of **60 to 120 seconds**, plus a document of **800 to 1200 words**.

### The video

It must use **at least three** of these, and you must say which:

- Generated stills
- Generated or animated video clips
- Generated voice narration
- An AI avatar
- Generated music
- AI-assisted editing, captions or cleanup
- An AI-assisted script

It must have **captions**, corrected by you.

It must carry a **visible disclosure** — on screen, in the description, or both. You decide which, and you justify the decision in the document.

The subject is yours. Something real is better: explain a concept from your studies, introduce a project, document something you made.

### The document

**1. The brief.** What the video is, who it is for, what it should achieve.

**2. What was AI-generated, and what was not.** A clear inventory. Every element, and which tool produced it. Anything you filmed, recorded, wrote or designed yourself, said plainly.

**3. The production account.** For each generated element:

- What you asked for
- **How many attempts, and how many were usable** — the hit rate
- What you had to fix
- What you abandoned as not good enough

The hit rate is marked. Honest numbers matter more than impressive ones.

**4. Your disclosure decision.** The section that carries the most weight.

- What exactly does your disclosure say, and where does it appear?
- Who is the audience, and what would they reasonably assume without it?
- What would be misleading if you said nothing?
- What did you decide **not** to disclose, and why is that defensible?

That last question is the interesting one. Nobody discloses every tool they used. Disclosing "I used spell check" is noise. The judgement is about what would change a viewer's understanding of what they are watching.

**5. What you would not do.** At least two things you could have done with these tools and chose not to. Real ones, with reasons. Cloning someone's voice, generating a recognisable person, presenting generated footage as real, using a synthetic presenter without saying so.

**6. Honest assessment.** Is the video good? Where did generative tools genuinely help, and where did they cost you more time than they saved? Which parts would have been better made conventionally?

## Rubric

Marked out of 100.

**The video, 25 marks.** Full marks for a finished, watchable, correctly captioned video using at least three generative techniques, where the techniques serve the content rather than being there to be counted. Marks lost for uncorrected captions, for a video that does not hold together, and for techniques included only to meet the minimum.

**Inventory, 15 marks.** Full marks for a complete, clear account of what was generated and what was not, naming tools. Marks lost for vagueness about any element, and heavily for anything a viewer would think was real that is not listed.

**Production account with hit rates, 20 marks.** Full marks for attempt counts, usable counts, fixes and abandonments for every generated element. Marks lost for impressions instead of numbers, and for an account with no failures in it, which is not believable.

**Disclosure decision, 25 marks.** Full marks for a specific disclosure, correctly placed, with a reasoned account of what the audience would assume, what would mislead, and what you deliberately did not disclose. This is the heaviest section. A submission with a disclosure but no reasoning behind it scores about half here.

**What you would not do, 10 marks.** Full marks for two specific, realistic refusals with reasons. Marks lost for hypotheticals nobody would have done anyway.

**Honest assessment, 5 marks.** Full marks for a genuine account of where the tools helped and where they did not.

## What will cost you marks

**No disclosure, or a disclosure with no reasoning.** The point of this assignment is the judgement, not the compliance.

**A production account with no failures.** Every one of these tools fails often. An account where everything worked first time reads as untested and loses marks across two sections.

**Generating a recognisable real person, or cloning a voice without consent.** This fails the assignment outright, whatever else is good about it.

**Uncorrected captions.** Names, terms and numbers are always wrong initially, and a large share of your viewers rely on them.

**Presenting generated footage as documentary.** If a viewer would take a generated clip as a record of something that happened, that needs disclosure regardless of what else you disclosed.

:::hint I do not know where the line is on disclosure
A practical test: imagine a viewer finds out afterwards exactly how the video was made. Would they feel misled? Generated background music: almost certainly not. A synthetic presenter they took for a real person: almost certainly yes. Generated footage of an event presented as having happened: definitely yes. AI-assisted editing of your own real footage: no. The line tracks what the viewer believed they were seeing, not how much AI was involved.
:::
